The Variegated scallop, Mimachlamys varia, attains a maximum shell height of 8 cm [Li = 8 cm], though field surveys across its European range typically record individuals measuring between 3 and 10 cm (3-10 cm) [Li = 3-10 cm]. This bivalve inhabits subtidal gravel and mixed-sediment beds, often attaching by byssal threads to shell debris or small stones. The asymptotic shell size is comparable to that of its congener Mimachlamys asperrima, though the latter may rarely exceed 9 cm in height. Somatic growth slows considerably after the onset of gametogenesis, and reported values for ultimate size are derived from the largest specimens collected during extensive dredge surveys in the English Channel and the Bay of Biscay. The species exhibits the pronounced shell sculpturing typical of pectinids, with 15 to 20 prominent radial ribs that contribute to structural strength and predator deterrence.

Sexual maturity in Mimachlamys varia is attained at a shell height of 5.75 cm [Lp = 5.75 cm], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of active gonad development and the capacity for external fertilisation. Individuals below this length are consistently found to lack mature gametes during histological examination. The size at puberty is somewhat lower than that recorded for the larger queen scallop Aequipecten opercularis, which matures closer to 6.5 cm, but is similar to other small-bodied pectinids in the same family. Once past this size, the spawning period extends from late spring through early autumn in most Atlantic populations, with peak reproductive activity observed in July and August when water temperatures are elevated.

At a rearing temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the embryonated egg of this scallop gives rise to a free-swimming trochophore larva after approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days], a rapid developmental rate that is typical of small-egg pectinids. The duration of embryonic development was established through controlled laboratory incubations at this constant thermal condition, with fertilised ova obtained from strip-spawned adults collected from natural beds. The resulting yolk-sac larva is lecithotrophic for a brief period before transitioning to planktotrophic feeding. The age at birth recorded here aligns with observations for the closely related Pecten maximus, which hatches in about 2 days at 18 °C, confirming that the slightly cooler temperature used for Mimachlamys varia does not markedly prolong this initial developmental stage.

The wet weight at birth for Mimachlamys varia is extremely small, estimated at approximately 0.000000164 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000000164 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of approximately 68 µm, which is typical of the size-corrected eggs of Aequipecten opercularis. This minute birth mass reflects the high fecundity characteristic of pectinids, which release large numbers of small, yolk-poor eggs into the water column. By contrast, the adult or ultimate wet weight reaches 31.7 grams [Wwi = 31.7 grams], indicating a massive increase in mass over the course of the lifespan. This adult body mass, calculated using a size-corrected allometric relationship from Aequipecten opercularis, is consistent with the moderately small body size of this species compared to the larger king scallop.

Laboratory trials conducted at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] determined that the free-swimming veliger larva of Mimachlamys varia undergoes metamorphosis after approximately 20 days from birth , a period that encompasses the transition from a ciliated, planktotrophic larva to a benthic, post-larval juvenile. The time since birth at settlement was measured in replicated larval rearing trials, where competence was confirmed by the appearance of a functional foot and the onset of substratum exploration. The maximum longevity of 7 years [am = 7 years] places this species among the shorter-lived pectinids, a pattern consistent with its small body size and high reproductive output, with the oldest individuals documented in a long-term population study in the Rade de Brest at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. Natural mortality typically follows senescence and a progressive decline in adductor muscle function.
